messages.subject: R & Basic Satistics
parts:
I recently joined this group in view of my interest to identify an
alternative to Microsoft Excel and the Analysis Add-in commonly used
for beginning statistics courses. Can anyone advise me if R and one
of its extensions will meet this need?

Thanks,

Rick

messages.author: c91a208fffacfb7e
messages.subject: Re: R & Basic Satistics
parts:
On Sat, Jan 16, 2010 at 8:40 AM, Rick <rava...@att.net> wrote:
> I recently joined this group in view of my interest to identify an
> alternative to Microsoft Excel and the Analysis Add-in commonly used
> for beginning statistics courses.  Can anyone advise me if R and one
> of its extensions will meet this need?

Using R in introductory statistics courses is a frequent topic on the
(high traffic) list R-h...@R-project.org. There is a specialized list
R-SIG-T...@R-project.org and you may want to check the archives of
that list rather than plunging into the rather formidable R-help list
archives. Follow the "Mailing lists" link on the left hand side of
www.R-project.org

There are several texts with some variation of titles containing
"introductory statistics" and "R", although I must admit that I
haven't found one that is entirely satisfactory and I have found at
least two that are unsatisfactory. (If you decide to follow up on
this I can tell you which books I would avoid and why.) Check the
books link on the left hand side of www.R-project.org where over 90
books are listed (most relate to advanced topics but some are at the
introductory level).

messages.author: d73eb13ab294801c
messages.subject: Re: R & Basic Satistics
parts:
Doug,

Yes, I am interested in learning of the introductory statistics texts
you refer to in your response. I was particularly interested in the R
book list you pointed out because of my background in physical
chemistry. Several of the more advanced books look worth reading.

Are you able to tell me anything regarding interaction with an
application exhibiting a similar relationship as that between Excel
and VBA? I like this relationship but it appears OpenOffice Calc may
accomplish this in a manner unique from the Microsoft method. I want
to pursue this further as well.

I am actually a returning student. I lost employment in May 2009 and
I'm taking prerequisites for a PA or DO degree. Our statistics
instructor recommended Excel 2003 or 2007 and I was hoping I could
accomplish all the goals of the course using OpenOffice Calc. From my
attempts to perform simple histograms and obtain descriptive
statistics for these to date this does not appear feasible. I was
surprised to learn this. I may have to research OpenOffice Calc
further.

Thanks,

Rick
